```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-studio-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> a search log, a concept matrix of 12 papers with an empty cell searched directly, a second-pass extraction sheet on the closest paper, and a gap statement with its evidence.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> the question below, two open databases (OpenAlex and one more, such as Semantic Scholar or Crossref, with the strings adapted to its search) and one review to snowball from.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> the rubric's bar for positioning: a concept matrix of at least 12 sources and a stated gap with evidence.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 30 minutes guided here, then about 4 hours on your own.</p>
</div>

<p><b>The worked question:</b> How do <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-expansion">capacity-expansion</span> models stand in for a whole year with a few <span class="lx-term" data-term="representative-period">representative periods</span>, and what happens to storage and to <span class="lx-term" data-term="extreme-period">extreme periods</span> when they do?</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Five search strings, OpenAlex titles and abstracts, 3 November 2026</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Change</th><th scope="col">String</th><th scope="col">Works</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Plain words</td><td><code>representative days capacity expansion</code></td><td class="n"><a href="https://openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:representative%20days%20capacity%20expansion">344</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>Quote one phrase, drop the model words (two changes)</td><td><code>&quot;representative days&quot;</code></td><td class="n"><a href="https://openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:%22representative%20days%22">649</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>Synonyms joined by OR</td><td><code>&quot;representative days&quot; OR &quot;representative periods&quot; OR &quot;time series aggregation&quot; OR &quot;typical days&quot;</code></td><td class="n"><a href="https://openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:%22representative%20days%22%20OR%20%22representative%20periods%22%20OR%20%22time%20series%20aggregation%22%20OR%20%22typical%20days%22">2,191</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>AND the model block</td><td><code>(&quot;representative days&quot; OR &quot;representative periods&quot; OR &quot;time series aggregation&quot; OR &quot;typical days&quot;) AND (&quot;capacity expansion&quot; OR &quot;generation expansion&quot; OR &quot;energy system model&quot; OR &quot;investment planning&quot;)</code></td><td class="n"><a href="https://openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:%28%22representative%20days%22%20OR%20%22representative%20periods%22%20OR%20%22time%20series%20aggregation%22%20OR%20%22typical%20days%22%29%20AND%20%28%22capacity%20expansion%22%20OR%20%22generation%20expansion%22%20OR%20%22energy%20system%20model%22%20OR%20%22investment%20planning%22%29">113</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>AND storage</td><td><code>(&quot;representative days&quot; OR &quot;representative periods&quot; OR &quot;time series aggregation&quot; OR &quot;typical days&quot;) AND (&quot;capacity expansion&quot; OR &quot;generation expansion&quot; OR &quot;energy system model&quot; OR &quot;investment planning&quot;) AND storage</code></td><td class="n"><a href="https://openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:%28%22representative%20days%22%20OR%20%22representative%20periods%22%20OR%20%22time%20series%20aggregation%22%20OR%20%22typical%20days%22%29%20AND%20%28%22capacity%20expansion%22%20OR%20%22generation%20expansion%22%20OR%20%22energy%20system%20model%22%20OR%20%22investment%20planning%22%29%20AND%20storage">49</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>The empty cell, searched directly</td><td><code>(&quot;representative days&quot; OR &quot;representative periods&quot; OR &quot;time series aggregation&quot; OR &quot;typical days&quot;) AND extreme AND storage</code></td><td class="n"><a href="https://openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:%28%22representative%20days%22%20OR%20%22representative%20periods%22%20OR%20%22time%20series%20aggregation%22%20OR%20%22typical%20days%22%29%20AND%20extreme%20AND%20storage">23</a></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-hint">Each count links the same search on OpenAlex's search page; counts there may differ as OpenAlex updates its records.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Moving the strings to a second database</p><p class="lx-hint">A string moves between databases only as far as their syntax allows. Log each search as you ran it there.</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Database</th><th scope="col">What its search takes</th><th scope="col">Log</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>OpenAlex</td><td>AND, OR, NOT and quoted phrases: this page's strings run unchanged.</td><td>String, field (titles and abstracts here), date, count.</td></tr><tr><td>Semantic Scholar</td><td>Quoted phrases, but no AND, OR or NOT on its search page: search one block's terms at a time. <span class="lx-hint">(its search FAQ, checked 8 November 2026)</span></td><td>Each search as typed, date, how many results you screened.</td></tr><tr><td>Crossref</td><td>No AND, OR or exact phrases: it ranks works by how well their records match your words. <span class="lx-hint">(Crossref's answer on its community forum, March 2023, checked 8 November 2026)</span></td><td>The words as typed, date, how many results you screened.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p>Snowballing from Hoffmann et al. (2020): 196 references (backward) and 229 citing works (forward) on 3 November 2026. Of the 12 matrix papers, the AND-the-model string finds 9, backward snowballing 9 and forward snowballing 1; together, all 12.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The concept matrix, coded from the abstracts (first pass)</p>
<p>The two ideas: a <span class="lx-term" data-term="storage-link">storage link</span> carries the energy stored at one period's end into the next; <span class="lx-term" data-term="extreme-period">extreme periods</span> are unusually demanding ones, such as high demand with little wind.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Tick a cell only when the abstract says so. “not stated” means the abstract does not say: it is not the same as no, and a second pass can change it. <b>yes</b>: the abstract reports it; <b>partly</b>: the abstract hints at it; <b>not stated</b>: the abstract does not say (not the same as no).</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Paper</th><th scope="col">Links storage between periods</th><th scope="col">Keeps extreme periods</th><th scope="col">Checks against a full-year run</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/tpwrs.2016.2596803">Poncelet et al. (2016)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Picks representative days with an optimization and compares it with <span class="lx-term" data-term="clustering">clustering</span> and simple rules, using new measures of how representative a set is.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.renene.2017.10.017">Kotzur et al. (2017)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Compares <span class="lx-term" data-term="time-series-aggregation">aggregation methods</span> across several energy-system designs; the system matters more than the method, and typical periods as usually modeled cannot carry seasonal storage.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>partly</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2017.03.051">Pfenninger (2017)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Compares downsampling, clustering and simple rules in a Great Britain power model with 25 years of wind and solar data; the best method depends on the data and the model.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>partly</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2018.01.023">Kotzur et al. (2018)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Links typical periods through a storage level that carries energy from one period to the next, so seasonal storage can be modeled, and compares with optimizing the full year.</span></td><td>yes</td><td>not stated</td><td>yes</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/tpwrs.2017.2746379">Liu, Sioshansi and Conejo (2017)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Picks representative days with two hierarchical clustering methods that keep correlations in time and between places, tested on the Texas power system against the full data.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>yes</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/tpwrs.2018.2819578">Tejada-Arango et al. (2018)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Adds links between representative days so that long-term storage fits an investment model, and benchmarks it against an hourly <span class="lx-term" data-term="unit-commitment">unit-commitment</span> model.</span></td><td>yes</td><td>not stated</td><td>yes</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2018.08.015">Mallapragada et al. (2018)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Compares a model with up to 12 representative days against a time-slice model for Texas, then runs both plans through an hourly operations model.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>yes</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2019.02.012">Teichgraeber and Brandt (2019)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Compares five clustering methods on two operating problems, battery and gas-turbine scheduling; a better clustering score does not always give a better result.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>partly</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/tpwrs.2019.2892619">Sun et al. (2019)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Groups days by the investment decisions each day would lead to, rather than by the input data alone, for large power systems with many locations.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2020.115224">Yeganefar et al. (2020)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Adds extreme days of high and low <span class="lx-term" data-term="net-demand">net load</span> to the representative days, picked with <span class="lx-term" data-term="self-organizing-map">self-organizing maps</span>, and tests them on two power systems.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>yes</td><td>partly</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2021.117696">Teichgraeber, Küpper and Brandt (2021)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Adds extreme periods one at a time, using the planning model's own results, until the design meets demand in every hour of the full data.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>yes</td><td>yes</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12667-022-00533-4">Reichenberg and Hedenus (2022)</a><br><span class="lx-hint">Measures how representative periods distort cost and capacity results against a full chronological year, in a European model where wind and solar supply 90% of generation.</span></td><td>not stated</td><td>not stated</td><td>yes</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>Abstracts reporting both a storage link and extreme periods: 0 papers (the empty cell). Storage link only: 2. Extreme periods only: 2. Neither stated: 8.</p>
<p>Searching that cell directly (the empty cell, searched directly) gave 23 works on 3 November 2026; at least 3 of them do both, by their abstracts: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2022.120624">Hilbers, Brayshaw and Gandy (2023)</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/powertech55446.2023.10202993">Moradi-Sepahvand and Tindemans (2023)</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epsr.2024.110788">Moradi-Sepahvand and Tindemans (2024)</a>. An empty cell is a lead, not a gap.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Reading the closest paper: Hilbers, Brayshaw and Gandy (2023)</p><ol>
<li><b>First pass</b> (5–10 min): Title, abstract, introduction, section headings, conclusions; glance at the references you already know. Out: The five Cs: category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity.</li>
<li><b>Second pass</b> (up to an hour): Figures, tables and the argument; skip the proofs. Mark the references to read next. Out: The extraction sheet, filled.</li>
<li><b>Third pass, optional</b> (4–5 hours for a beginner, outside this studio's 4 hours): Rebuild the work under the same assumptions, and challenge each one. Out: What you would do differently, and what it would change.</li>
</ol><p>Its headings (open preprint, October 2022), for the first pass:</p><ul><li>1. Introduction (capacity expansion planning; time series aggregation; inter-period links and storage)</li><li>2. This paper's contribution</li><li>3. Methods (overview; framework; remarks)</li><li>4. Simulation studies (overview; setup; validation; example; discussion)</li><li>5. Conclusions (conclusions; extensions)</li></ul>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>The first pass, worked: the five Cs</summary><dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Category</dt><dd>What kind of paper is it? A methods paper: a new aggregation framework, tested in simulations on a six-region test system.</dd><dt>Context</dt><dd>Which papers does it build on? Two from your matrix: Kotzur et al. (2018) for linked storage, and Teichgraeber, Küpper and Brandt (2021) for extreme periods taken from model results.</dd><dt>Correctness</dt><dd>Which assumptions will you check in pass two? A test system based on the IEEE six-bus system; demand and wind only, no solar; operation with <span class="lx-term" data-term="perfect-foresight">perfect foresight</span>.</dd><dt>Contributions</dt><dd>What is new? Periods chosen after a first model run that keep chronology for storage and keep the extreme periods that drive capacity; models, data and code released.</dd><dt>Clarity</dt><dd>Is it well written? Your judgment: note one thing you would ask the authors.</dd></dl></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>The second pass, worked: the extraction sheet</summary><dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Question</dt><dd>Can choosing periods after a first model run cut the error of capacity plans built from long weather series, in models with storage?</dd><dt>Scale and boundary</dt><dd>A six-region test grid: baseload, peaking and wind generation, transmission and storage, built from scratch.</dd><dt>Data vintage</dt><dd>Hourly demand and wind for European countries, 1980–2017, from a published <span class="lx-term" data-term="reanalysis">reanalysis</span>-based dataset.</dd><dt>Method</dt><dd>Plan on representative days chosen from the input data; run operations over the full series; use those results to choose new periods, extreme and regular; plan again.</dd><dt>Counterfactual</dt><dd>Three conventional schemes chosen from the input data alone and, on 3-year samples, the plan from the full series.</dd><dt>Sensitivity and validation</dt><dd>30 and 120 representative days; 40 resampled series; unserved energy checked over the full series.</dd><dt>Not modeled</dt><dd>Solar; operation without <span class="lx-term" data-term="perfect-foresight">perfect foresight</span> (named by the authors as an extension).</dd><dt>Code and data</dt><dd>Public, with a Zenodo DOI.</dd></dl><p class="lx-hint">Worked from the open preprint (October 2022); the published version is at the DOI above.</p></details>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Write the gap statement</p><p>Draft your gap statement: what you searched (where, when, strings), what the matrix shows, what the direct search found, what a second pass on the closest paper showed, and the question that remains.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Your own literature map: about 4 hours</p><ol><li>Write two concept blocks for your own question; run five logged strings in OpenAlex, then adapt them to a second database's syntax (string as run, date, count). (30 min)</li><li>Screen titles and abstracts down to about 30 candidates; note why you dropped the rest. (30 min)</li><li>Find one review; snowball backward and forward from it; add what the searches missed. (30 min)</li><li>Do a first pass on 12 papers (about 7 minutes each) and code them in a concept matrix with a written coding rule. (90 min)</li><li>Search your empty cell directly and log the string, date and count. (15 min)</li><li>Read the closest paper in a second pass, fill the extraction sheet, then write the gap statement. (45 min)</li></ol><p class="lx-hint">Optional, beyond the 4 hours: a third pass on the closest paper (4–5 hours for a beginner).</p>
<!-- r02-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you build the strings yourself, predict each count, code four papers and test the empty cell step by step; your drafts stay in this browser.</p>
```

## Two answers to the same task
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r02-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r02-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak answer · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Representative periods are widely used, but few studies [1] consider storage and extreme events together [2]. This study is the first [3] to fill this gap [4].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> No count, no database, no date: a reader cannot check it.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> Undefined: linked between periods? Extremes chosen how?</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> A novelty claim the evidence cannot carry; a direct search finds at least three papers that do both.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> Asserted, not shown: no matrix, no search of the cell.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong answer · Proficient</p><p class="lx-ex-lines"><b>Search:</b> OpenAlex titles and abstracts, 3 November 2026, five logged strings [1]; one review snowballed both ways [2].
<b>Matrix:</b> 12 papers coded from their abstracts by a written rule [3]; no abstract reports both a storage link and extreme periods [4].
<b>Direct check:</b> a search of that cell returned 23 works; by their abstracts, at least three do both [5] (Hilbers et al. 2023; Moradi-Sepahvand and Tindemans 2023, 2024).
<b>Closest work:</b> a second pass on Hilbers et al. finds a six-region test grid with demand and wind only, no solar [6].
<b>Remaining question:</b> does choosing periods after a first model run still keep extremes and storage right once solar is added? The two other papers get a second pass before we claim it [7].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Database, date and strings: anyone can repeat the search and see what has changed since.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> Search and snowballing find different papers; together they found all twelve.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> The rubric's bar for positioning: at least 12 sources, coded with a stated rule.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> Said as the coding allows: what the abstracts report, not what the papers lack.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> The empty cell is tested, not assumed, and the gap as first stated does not survive.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> The closest work is read, not just named: the extraction sheet supplies the distinction.</li><li value="7"><b>Works:</b> A narrowed gap with its evidence, held as provisional: Proficient. Strong needs the other two read and the gap to survive a reviewer's search.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak answer</th><th scope="col">Strong answer</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Evidence</th><td>None given</td><td>Search log, review, matrix of 12</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">The empty cell</th><td>Assumed to be a gap</td><td>Searched directly: 23 works, at least 3 do both</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">After the check</th><td>&quot;The first&quot;</td><td>No novelty claim; a narrowed question, tied to the closest work's second pass</td></tr></tbody></table>
<!-- r02-exemplars:end -->
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Search</dt><dd>Synonyms inside a block with OR, blocks joined with AND, phrases in quotes; log the database, string, date and count.</dd>
<dt>Snowball</dt><dd>Backward through a review's references, forward through the works that cite it: each finds papers a search misses.</dd>
<dt>Matrix</dt><dd>Papers in rows, ideas in columns, coded by a written rule; an empty cell is a lead.</dd>
<dt>Test the cell</dt><dd>Search the empty cell directly before calling it a gap, then read the closest work in two passes.</dd>
<dt>Abstracts only</dt><dd>A first-pass matrix records what abstracts report; “not stated” is not “no”.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>Why the course never calls a question “novel”</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>Few papers on a topic is not evidence that a question is new, important or feasible. It can mean:</p>
<ul>
<li>the field uses other words;</li>
<li>the field is small;</li>
<li>the question was tried and dropped.</li>
</ul>
<p>The rubric asks for a gap stated with evidence; its Strong level asks that the gap survive a reviewer's search.</p>
<p>The question studio (<a href="r10-question-studio.html">R10</a>) shows how much has been written on a topic only as context, for the same reason.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>The same workflow for other question types</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>The twelve papers here share one method family, optimization models. That is this example's choice, not the studio's: optimization is one family among several (<a href="r03-system-and-method.html">R3</a>).</p>
<p>Search, snowballing and the matrix work for every question type (<a href="r01-framing.html">R1</a>). Only the matrix columns change, to fit the evidence each type uses. The questions below are illustrative.</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Type</th><th scope="col">Question</th><th scope="col">Matrix columns</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Descriptive</td><td>How often did a region's wind output stay under a tenth of its capacity for a whole day?</td><td>Data source and years · time resolution · how a low day is defined</td></tr>
<tr><td>Explanatory</td><td>Why did members of some rural co-ops adopt rooftop solar faster than others?</td><td>Data (survey, records, interviews) · method (statistics, case study) · setting</td></tr>
<tr><td>Evaluative</td><td>Did a time-of-use tariff lower household peak demand, compared with a flat rate?</td><td>Comparison group · design (trial, difference-in-differences, matching) · metered or surveyed</td></tr>
<tr><td>Predictive</td><td>What will a city's summer peak demand be in ten years, and with what uncertainty?</td><td>Forecast method · how uncertainty is shown · validation period</td></tr>
<tr><td>Descriptive, qualitative evidence</td><td>How do households describe their winter heating choices?</td><td>Who was asked, and how many · interviews or documents · how answers were coded</td></tr>
<tr><td>Prescriptive</td><td>Which mix of storage and transmission should a region build to meet a 2035 target?</td><td>Method family (optimization, simulation, multi-criteria) · objective and limits · how uncertainty is handled</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Systematic reviews with a registered protocol, two independent screeners and a flow diagram of every record: the next step when a review is itself the study.</li>
<li>Reference managers: any one works if it stores the DOI, your tags and the date you added each paper.</li>
<li>Gray literature (agency reports, grid-operator studies): search the agencies' own sites and log them the same way.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>From this map to your capstone proposal</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>The capstone research project starts from a typed question (<a href="r01-framing.html">R1</a>) and needs this studio's matrix and gap statement in its proposal.</p>
<p>The closest prior work you found here becomes your reference point when you build and check your analysis (<a href="r04-data.html">R4</a>, then <a href="r05-build-validate.html">R5</a>): a benchmark for a model, a comparison study for empirical work.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<tr><td class="n">Semantic Scholar</td><td>An open database for the second search in your log. Its search page takes quoted phrases but not AND, OR or NOT, so search one block's terms at a time.</td><td class="s">semanticscholar.org · its search FAQ, checked 8 November 2026</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">Crossref</td><td>Open metadata of works with DOIs. Its search ranks records by your words and takes no AND, OR or exact phrases: good for checking DOIs and catching missed works.</td><td class="s">search.crossref.org · its community forum, March 2023, checked 8 November 2026</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">Google Scholar</td><td>Free to search but not open, and with no API: log the words, the date and how many results you screened.</td><td class="s">scholar.google.com</td></tr>
```
